transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-30 16:00 PT
Duration: ~56 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Aaron (Redwood SE), Liam (CTO), Priya (ML), Evan (Infra)

Summary: quick perf deep dive, focus on continuous batching and scheduler knobs. Customer wants 50-75ms p50 and p99 under 400ms for short chats, plus ability to scale to 2000 rps during peak with mixed short/long requests.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros, then Aaron will walk through tuning knobs.
[00:20] Liam: hi, thanks. our goal is basically predictable p99 under 400 for the shortest flows. we run a mix — ~70% short chats (20-60 tokens) and 30% longer (200+ tokens).
[00:40] Aaron: cool, that mix is important. we'll focus on the scheduler, continuous batching, and max_num_seqs since those have the biggest throughput impact for small tokens.
[01:05] Priya: one note — our current internal model runs on 8xA10g and we saw unpredictable latency spikes when the KV cache isn't warm.
[01:25] Aaron: yeah, KV-cache warmup is a common culprit. two things: prefix caching and keeping hot KV shards pinned. we'll show a warmup routine in the bench script.
[01:50] Evan: also curious about quantization — we tried 4-bit and saw a slight quality drop on instruction-following; is that expected?
[02:10] Aaron: possible. 4-bit (QLoRA-style / custom quant) reduces memory and can improve throughput but sometimes hurts generation stability. for brightscale's short chats maybe 8-bit is safer unless you run evals.
[02:35] Maya: important to map quality thresholds to which quant profiles we recommend.

[03:00] Aaron: ok scheduler knobs — first, continuous batching, which is our default approach: the runtime aggregates incoming sequences into a live batch up to max_batch_tokens or max_num_seqs and dispatches either on a fullness threshold or a deadline. knobs are: max_num_seqs, max_batch_tokens, and delay_ms (deadline).
[03:30] Liam: what's a typical delay_ms? we can't introduce >50ms overhead on short requests.
[03:45] Aaron: for low-latency flows we set delay_ms to 10-20ms with max_num_seqs 6-8 for small tokens. that keeps p50 low and increases pack efficiency. raising max_num_seqs to 12 helps throughput but hurts p50.
[04:10] Priya: so max_num_seqs=8 is a sweet spot?
[04:18] Aaron: for your mix yes. also set max_batch_tokens to something like 8k to cover a few long requests without blocking.

[04:45] Aaron: another trick is adaptive deadlines: when backlog is high, deadline goes to 0 (immediate dispatch) and rely on larger batch sizes; when idle, allow a small delay to pack.
[05:05] Evan: do you expose a scheduler mode per-route? we have different SLAs per endpoint.
[05:15] Aaron: yes, Redwood supports per-route scheduler policies — you can pin policies by route or model variant. so chat-short-route can use delay_ms 12 / max_num_seqs 8, while long-gen-route can use higher max_num_seqs and larger delay_ms.

[05:40] Liam: benching: what synthetic distribution should we run?
[05:45] Aaron: we'll send a bench harness. recommended: 70/30 short/long, token distributions matching your telemetry; ramp concurrency to target RPS, warm KV cache for 5-10 minutes before measuring, run 5-minute steady windows to capture p99.

[06:15] Priya: about KV cache — how big should warm cache be? we have user prefixes that vary; we can pre-populate common prefixes but not everything.
[06:30] Aaron: focus on hot prefixes and frequent session contexts. also the runtime supports partial KV-cache reads; ensure prefix alignment in your prompt templates to maximize reuse. we also recommend a small keep-alive pool to avoid cold-starts for low-volume tenants.

[07:00] Aaron: token limits: cap max_input_tokens per request to prevent runaway long requests taking a slot. and use token accounting for batching (so a 300-token request counts appropriately).
[07:25] Evan: if we cap inputs to 512 tokens, long flows will be truncated — acceptable for most. but some flows rely on long context; can we offload to separate long-context workers?
[07:40] Aaron: yep, separate worker pools for long-context models is common. you can route long requests to dedicated capacity with higher max_batch_tokens and lower preemption.

[08:10] Liam: curious about p99 tradeoff vs batch size — can you show numbers?
[08:18] Aaron: we pulled example numbers from similar customers: with max_num_seqs=4 and delay 15ms, short token p50=22ms, p99~210ms at 800 rps. increasing max_num_seqs to 8 improved throughput by ~35% but p50 rose to ~35ms and p99 to ~320ms. those are illustrative.
[08:45] Priya: we need to hit 50-75ms p50 and p99 < 400 at peaks; sounds feasible with max_num_seqs=6-8 and small delay.

[09:05] Aaron: quantization: if you need to squeeze more capacity per GPU look at 4-bit mixed with per-kernel tuning. some kernels run faster quantized; others slower. our optimizer picks kernel variants per sequence length and quant profile.
[09:30] Evan: is kernel selection deterministic? sometimes our runs had jitter.
[09:40] Aaron: kernel selection is deterministic given sequence length and quant, but there is runtime scheduling interplay (GPU contention, memory bandwidth) that adds jitter. we instrument per-token latency in the console to help debug.

[10:05] Liam: can we run this in our VPC? we need private deployment for compliance.
[10:15] Maya: yes, Redwood Private supports VPC peering and an on-prem package. key considerations: egress rules for model artifacts, KMS integration, and observability endpoints.
[10:35] Evan: any network latency impacts for KV cache if control plane is separate?
[10:45] Aaron: KV cache is local to the serving nodes; control plane interactions are minimal. network hop for metrics/logs can add a few ms but not in the critical path. if you run fully on-prem, you avoid cloud egress and get lower variance.

[11:15] Priya: about warmup script details?
[11:20] Aaron: bench script will do: 1) pre-warm KV by replaying top 10k prefixes, 2) ramp to 50% RPS for 3 minutes, 3) steady at target for 5 minutes, 4) capture p50/p95/p99 and per-token breakdown. we'll share the repo link.
[11:45] Liam: please include hooks for variable token lengths and concurrency patterns.

[12:10] Aaron: autoscaling knobs: for Dedicated pools we suggest CPU/GPU metrics-based scaling and request queue depth triggers. avoid too-aggressive downscaling; keep a small buffer for burst.
[12:35] Evan: how does burst capacity work? we might need 2-3x burst during launches.
[12:45] Maya: Dedicated has burst credits with configured burst instances; we can size that in the proposal.

[13:05] Priya: can we control batching behavior at inference call-time? e.g., pass priority header?
[13:15] Aaron: yes we support priority lanes. High-priority calls can get preemptive scheduling semantics with lower delay and reserved tokens. That helps for admin/interactive flows.

[13:40] Aaron: pitfalls: 1) setting max_num_seqs too high will increase p50; 2) cold KV cache causes p99 spikes; 3) overly aggressive quant without eval can regress quality.

[14:00] Liam: for the bench we'd like to test 3 configs: conservative (max_num_seqs=4), balanced (6-8), aggressive throughput (12). can you enumerate expected resource differences?
[14:15] Aaron: yes — aggressive will require ~30-40% fewer GPUs but will have higher latency variance. balanced is usually best for mixed workloads. we'll add GPU counts to the bench results.

[14:40] Maya: quick note on observability — in console you'll get token-level cost, per-route p99 and trace ids to correlate spikes to payloads.
[14:55] Evan: good, we need trace ids tied into our Sentry.

[15:10] Aaron: one more: scheduler backpressure. if queue grows, we prefer immediate dispatch and routing to a larger model variant or fallback to a cheaper model to maintain SLOs. that's part of our smart routing policy.

[15:40] Priya: fallback sounds useful. can we set percentile-based fallback? e.g., if p95 > 350ms fallback to smaller model?
[15:50] Aaron: yes, you can set dynamic policies by percentile and route. we can demo this in a follow-up.

[16:10] Liam: anything on request shaping? like token pooling or request coalescing?
[16:20] Aaron: request coalescing at the client layer helps a lot — batch multiple short messages into one call when latency budget allows. also use prompt templates to canonicalize prefixes to maximize KV hits.

[16:45] Evan: concerns about memory fragmentation with many sequence lengths?
[16:55] Aaron: we mitigate using slab allocators and consistent eviction policies; still, very heterogenous lengths increase fragmentation and reduce packing efficiency. recommend quantizing request sizes or capping extremes.

[17:20] Priya: what about multi-tenant isolation? we need guaranteed capacity for certain customers.
[17:30] Aaron: Dedicated supports tenant pinning and quota reservations; for Private you can set namespaces and resource quotas. default is best-effort but can be locked down.

[17:55] Aaron: to summarize bench plan: warm KV -> run 3 configs (4, 8, 12) -> capture p50/p95/p99 and GPU usage -> include quant profiles.

[18:10] Liam: timeline and next steps look good. any blockers?
[18:15] Evan: network / firewall confirmation from our infra team.

[18:20] Priya: telemetry export to our metrics pipeline to correlate traces.

[18:30] Maya: we'll send the bench harness link and a sample results template. Aaron will own the bench script share.

[18:40] Aaron: I'll include scripts for KV warmup and a sample set of prefixes. also include a short README on recommended scheduler settings per-route.

[18:55] Liam: ok thanks. one last Q — do you have example memory footprints for 8xA10g vs 4xH100 for the balanced config?
[19:10] Aaron: rough numbers: with 8-bit quant, an 8xA10g pool can handle ~1.2M tokens/sec for mixed traffic; 4xH100 at TF32/quantized kernels will be ~1.6-1.9x that, depends on seq length. we'll add a sizing appendix.

[19:40] Priya: that'll help procurement.

[20:00] Maya: ok let's wrap and recap.
[20:05] Aaron: action items — I'll share bench and we agreed on dates.
[20:15] Liam: thanks everyone.

-- End of recorded portion --

Notes: transcript is auto-generated; contains occasional mis-words (e.g., 4-bit/pro files may appear as "for-bit"), speaker labels approximate. Links shared: bench harness repo (link in follow-up), Redwood scheduler knobs doc, Dedicated sizing spreadsheet.
